clue.text: Fifty pence 'entertaining' Everyman's spent

indicators.note: To entertain a guest is to have them inside the house, so what follows is kept within rather than set beside.

parts.note: L is fifty in Roman numerals
Everyman is the setter, and a setter speaking of himself says I, so Everyman's is I'm
p is the coin's own abbreviation, as in 50p

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs his own clues most weeks, and the trick is always the same one: his name is standing in for the word I.
explanation.definitionFit: spent → LIMP: the sense of a runner at the finish, drained of all stiffness rather than merely tired.

clue.text: Organised routine do, and cleared up

indicators.note: To organise is to put things into an order somebody chose, and the order chosen is never the one they arrived in.

parts.note: the nine letters of ROUTINE DO, set out afresh

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an office party being planned, and the definition is the last two words, which read as more of the same sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: cleared up → IRONED OUT: the laundry metaphor, where a wrinkle in a plan is pressed flat until nothing catches on it.

clue.text: Urges drinks

definitions.meaning: to press somebody is to urge them, as in pressing a guest to stay for one more
the other sense is the pressé, the bottled drink of pressed fruit that turns up as elderflower or ginger

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two dictionaries, and no wordplay to hunt for. The second sense comes from the French for pressed and reached English through a menu.
explanation.definitionFit: Urges → PRESSES, as pressing a point is urging it; drinks → PRESSES, a pressé being a drink of pressed fruit.

clue.text: Condition in which frost becomes frothed?

definitions.text: Condition in which frost becomes frothed?

parts.note: read as weather it goes nowhere, since a hard freeze does not turn into foam
not a state of the air but of the mouth, and the two words are the same word said two ways

explanation.walkthrough: There are no letters to assemble. Say the first word with the speech fault the answer names and what comes out is the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is the definition: the speech habit turns every s into a th, so frost leaves the mouth sounding like frothed.

clue.text: In vague sense, how post-diet clothes fit

definitions.meaning: the figurative use: an approximate way of speaking, where the words are not meant to be pinned down precisely
the literal use: slack, with room to spare between the cloth and the wearer

explanation.walkthrough: One adverb pulling in two directions — imprecision and slackness — which are the same idea applied to words and to cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves are one adverb: speaking in a vague sense is speaking without a tight fit to the facts, exactly as slack clothing hangs.

clue.text: Vacuous silly academic getting promotion in ecclesiastical council

indicators.note: A promotion lifts you up the ladder, and in a down clue a word lifted up is read from the bottom.
Something vacuous is hollow, empty through the middle, so the word beside it keeps only the letters at its two ends.

parts.note: silly hollowed out keeps only its first and last letters
an academic is a don, and raised up the column DON reads NOD

explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' is the crossword's word for any academic, Oxbridge or not, and being three letters it nearly always arrives turned round or buried.
explanation.definitionFit: ecclesiastical council → SYNOD: the assembly of clergy that governs a church, that body's own name for its parliament.

clue.text: We hear of harder breastbones

indicators.note: What we hear is not what is written down, so the match the clue wants is a match of sound alone.

parts.note: harder is sterner, and said aloud that word lands on the Latin plural of sternum

explanation.walkthrough: English lets the r at the end of sterner go unsounded, which is the whole reason a comparative adjective and an anatomical plural can share a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: breastbones → STERNA: the sternum is the flat bone down the front of the chest, and anatomy keeps its Latin plural.

clue.text: Agreement accepted by leprechaun is ongoing

indicators.note: To accept a thing is to take it in and hold it, so the letters are already sitting inside the words that follow.

parts.note: the run crosses three words: the tail of 'leprechaun', the whole of 'is', and the front of 'ongoing'

explanation.walkthrough: A hidden answer that spans three words is the hardest kind to spot, because the eye reads whole words before it reads letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Agreement → UNISON: singing in unison is everybody on one note, and the word carried that sense across to people who think alike.

clue.text: Swagger, as sax player will do

definitions.meaning: the figurative sense: to boast, to talk yourself up in company
the literal reading, where the horn is the instrument and the tooting is simply playing it

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that a saxophonist does this without boasting at all: the instrument really is his, and blowing it is the job.
explanation.definitionFit: Swagger names the phrase's boastful sense; the other half is the literal one, a player blowing an instrument that belongs to him.

clue.text: Happy — formerly — to take in brash nephew at home

indicators.note: A household that takes somebody in puts them up within its walls, so everything named next goes inside the word before.

parts.note: formerly is once, and it opens up after its third letter to make room
a brash person is a loud one
nephew is shortened to its own first letter here, the way a family tree writes it
somebody at home is in, which is the crossword's favourite two letters for it

explanation.walkthrough: Three separate pieces go into the one gap, which is why the dashes are worth noticing: they fence 'formerly' off as the word being opened.
explanation.definitionFit: Happy → ON CLOUD NINE: the idiom for elation so complete that it lifts you off the ground, far past merely pleased.

clue.text: Dancing upon the sand? That's easily solved

indicators.note: Dancers keep swapping places with one another, and letters set dancing do exactly that to their order.

parts.note: the eleven letters of UPON THE SAND, re-laid

explanation.walkthrough: A beach scene turns into a courtroom verdict. The enumeration's hyphens are the clue that the answer is one adjective and not three words.
explanation.definitionFit: easily solved → OPEN-AND-SHUT: said of a case whose evidence settles it at once, leaving no argument to be had.

clue.text: Horses for children who ride motorbikes?

definitions.meaning: a rocker is a rocking horse, the nursery toy mounted on curved runners
the leather-jacketed bikers of the sixties, the mods' opposite number

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are British and both are dated, which is the setter's joke: a nursery toy and a seaside gang, and one word for the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Horses for children → ROCKERS as rocking horses; who ride motorbikes → ROCKERS, the sixties bikers who fought mods at seaside resorts.

clue.text: Like Billy-No-Mates, Friday's gone — going on forever

indicators.note: What has gone is no longer there, so the letters named beside it are simply never written down.

parts.note: Billy No-Mates has no friends at all, so being like him is being FRIENDLESS, and seven of those letters survive
Fri is the diary's abbreviation for Friday, and those three letters come off the front

explanation.walkthrough: The dash is doing the work of an equals sign: everything to the left of it builds the word and everything to the right defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: going on forever → ENDLESS: having no end to reach, in time or in patience, which is a stronger claim than merely long.

clue.text: Morals you declined in licentious manner

indicators.note: A thing that has declined has slipped from the state it was in, and these letters have slipped out of the order they were given.

parts.note: the nine letters of MORALS YOU, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The surface says somebody turned down an offer of principles; the wordplay says the principles themselves came apart.
explanation.definitionFit: in licentious manner → AMOROUSLY: acting out of desire rather than affection, the adverb wanted when the love is the improper kind.

clue.text: Depicted as haggard

definitions.meaning: the artist's sense: set down in pencil or ink
the face's sense: pulled tight and hollow by strain or illness

explanation.walkthrough: Both come off the same verb to pull — a line pulled across paper, a face pulled thin — which is why one word can carry them.
explanation.definitionFit: Depicted → DRAWN in the sense of sketched; haggard → DRAWN as a face is, tightened and gaunt with strain.

clue.text: Sinfulness in drunken VE Day trip

indicators.note: Somebody drunken cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state will not hold the line they were given either.

parts.note: the nine letters of VE DAY TRIP, reordered

explanation.walkthrough: VE Day is the eighth of May 1945, so the surface is a street party outing — exactly the innocent picture the definition is not describing.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinfulness → DEPRAVITY: moral corruption of the settled kind, a character gone bad rather than one lapse.

clue.text: Military trainee's dishonourable type — and French

parts.note: a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably, the old word for one
et is the French for and

explanation.walkthrough: A clue in two halves with the join hidden inside an apostrophe. Naming a language after a word is the standard way of asking for its translation.
explanation.definitionFit: Military trainee → CADET: a young officer under instruction, still learning the trade rather than holding a commission in it.

clue.text: Delicious serving of gazpacho I celebrated

indicators.note: A serving is a helping taken out of something larger, so only part of what follows is wanted.

parts.note: the run crosses three words: the tail of 'gazpacho', the whole of 'I', and the front of 'celebrated'

explanation.walkthrough: A one-letter word in the middle is the best cover a hidden answer can have, because the eye treats a lone 'I' almost as punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: Delicious → CHOICE: the grocer's sense of picked out as the best of the crop, which is how a choice cut earns its name.

clue.text: Australian pointed rudely, son — here?

definitions.note: The Antipodes is a plural-looking name for one region, so a bare 'here' points at it as it would point at any single place.

indicators.note: To do a thing rudely is to do it with no respect for how it ought to be done, and letters handled that way come back out of order.

parts.note: A is the single-letter abbreviation for Australia
the seven letters of POINTED, shuffled
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.walkthrough: The dash sets the definition apart, and 'here' is asked from wherever the reader happens to be sitting — each hemisphere is the other's far side.
explanation.definitionFit: here? → ANTIPODES: the region diametrically opposite your own, so which end of the world it names depends on who is asking.

clue.text: Revelled topless, titillated

indicators.note: The top of a down entry is the letter standing at its head, and topless says that letter is missing.

parts.note: revelled is CAROUSED, and with the C at its head gone these seven letters remain

explanation.walkthrough: Carouse for revel is a word crosswords keep alive almost single-handed, and here the surface leans on the racier sense of all three words at once.
explanation.definitionFit: titillated → AROUSED: a plain synonym at the milder end, to arouse being to stir feeling, with titillate naming the kind stirred.

clue.text: Reveal ultimately stylish line of stitching included in source of wool

indicators.note: Whatever is included in a thing sits within its boundaries, so the letters before it go inside the word after it.

parts.note: a tup is a ram, and the fleece comes off him

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes at the very end, so the letter wanted is the one the word finishes on.

parts.note: the letter stylish finishes on
stitches are worked in rows

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tup' for a ram is worth banking: setters reach for it whenever they want a T and a P with a gap open between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Reveal → THROW UP: the sense in 'the search threw up new evidence' — to bring something to the surface where it can be seen.

clue.text: Good to visit Impressionist retrospective that's hung slackly

indicators.note: A visitor comes inside the house, so the letter doing the visiting goes within the word it calls on.
A retrospective looks back over what came before, and a word looked back over is read the other way round.

parts.note: the Impressionist is Degas, and his name looked back over gives these five letters
G is the standard abbreviation for good, as on a school report

explanation.walkthrough: A painter's name is raw material as often as it is a person, and 'retrospective' is doing gallery duty on the surface and letter duty underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: hung slackly → SAGGED: what a rope or a hemline does when nothing holds it taut, sinking in the middle under its own weight.

clue.text: Orion arranged company for river to the Atlantic

indicators.note: To arrange is to settle things into an order of your own choosing, which is not the order they came in.

parts.note: the five letters of the hunter's name, reordered
Co is the abbreviation on any firm's letterhead

explanation.walkthrough: A constellation turns into a waterway with one letter moved, and the definition is exact rather than decorative: this one does not feed the Amazon.
explanation.definitionFit: river to the Atlantic → ORINOCO: the great Venezuelan waterway, emptying through a huge delta into the ocean's western edge.

clue.text: Confess painful response as joke backfires

indicators.note: Something that backfires comes out of the wrong end, and a word sent that way is read from its last letter first.

parts.note: the noise you make when something hurts
a joke made on words is a pun, turned round here

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a gag falling flat; the wordplay has the same word doing it literally, which is about as neat as a five-letter clue gets.
explanation.definitionFit: Confess → OWN UP: the phrasal verb for admitting a fault, where own means acknowledge as yours rather than possess.

clue.text: Primarily 'ravenous', offensively avaricious driver hindering others gallingly?

definitions.text: 'ravenous', offensively avaricious driver hindering others gallingly?

indicators.note: What is primary stands first, so what is taken from each word is the letter at its head.

parts.words: 'ravenous', offensively avaricious driver hindering others gallingly
parts.note: the initials of the seven words in order: ravenous, offensively, avaricious, driver, hindering, others, gallingly

explanation.walkthrough: Seven words, seven initials, and the sentence still describes the answer exactly. The quotation marks round the first word are pure surface decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a driver who takes more than his share of the road and holds up everyone stuck behind.

clue.text: Spotless: all hesitance was resolved

indicators.note: To resolve something is to break it down into the parts it is made of, and parts broken out can be put back in any order.

parts.note: the fifteen letters of ALL HESITANCE WAS, rebuilt

explanation.walkthrough: The colon stands in for an equals sign, so the one word before it is the meaning and everything after it is the machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotless → CLEAN AS A WHISTLE: the idiom for something with nothing whatever on it, used of a criminal record as readily as of a kitchen.

clue.text: Small dish that's sweet potato

parts.note: S is the clothing label's abbreviation for small
pud is short for pudding, the sweet course at the end of a meal

explanation.walkthrough: Two abbreviations inside four squares. 'Sweet' as a noun is the British word for dessert, which is what makes the pudding reading fair.
explanation.definitionFit: potato → SPUD: the everyday informal name for one, borrowed from the spade-like tool once used to dig them up.

clue.text: After line cut, theatre work is profitable

indicators.note: To cut a thing is to take a piece off it, and what is taken off here is the single letter named just before.

parts.note: the work put on in a theatre is PLAYS, and with the L cut out these four letters remain
l is the standard abbreviation for line, as in a poem's l.4

explanation.walkthrough: An actor's line and a printed line share one abbreviation, and the theatrical surface is built to make you read the wrong one.
explanation.definitionFit: is profitable → PAYS: the intransitive sense in 'crime doesn't pay', where the activity itself returns more than it costs.
